Neonatal Starry smooth-hounds emerge from their mother at a total length of approximately 33 cm [Lb = approximately 33 cm], a size that reflects the constraints of yolk-dependent development within the oviduct. This modest length at birth, typical of small-bodied triakid sharks, positions pups to begin foraging immediately on small benthic crustaceans and cephalopods. Growth proceeds steadily during the early juvenile phase, with individuals adding length through active feeding in coastal nursery grounds. The species is characterized by a notable ultimate total length of 140 cm [Li = 140 cm], a maximum size that distinguishes adult females as the larger sex in most populations. Males tend to remain somewhat smaller on average, though the largest recorded specimens of either sex rarely exceed this total length threshold. Field measurements from the northeast Atlantic indicate that adults achieving this ultimate size are typically older individuals that have accumulated length incrementally over many years. The ability to reach such a length requires sustained access to productive foraging habitats and low rates of natural mortality, conditions that are met in certain protected shelf regions but may be compromised in areas subject to heavy fishing pressure.

Males of this species reach sexual maturation at a total length of 75 cm [Lp = 75 cm], a milestone that typically occurs several years before females begin pupping. In contrast, females generally attain reproductive maturity at a larger body size of 80 cm [Lp = 80 cm], reflecting the greater structural requirements for gestation and the energetic demands of producing litters of 7 to 15 pups per reproductive event [N_R_i = 7 to 15 pups per reproductive event]. This litter size is consistent with estimates for other members of the genus Mustelus and suggests a reproductive strategy that balances moderate fecundity against the advantages of producing relatively large, well-developed neonates. The timing of these maturation events is influenced by local thermal conditions and food availability, with individuals in warmer, more productive waters reaching the requisite size thresholds earlier than those in cooler regions.

Data from captive studies and field-tagging programs, conducted at a stable water temperature of 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C], have provided key insights into the species' early life history. The gestation period, defined here as the age at birth, spans approximately 657 days [ab = approximately 657 days] under these thermal conditions, a protracted embryonic phase that aligns with the slow developmental rates characteristic of temperate elasmobranchs at a temperature of 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C]. This length of gestation is based on an inferred embryonic growth rate of roughly 0.3 cm per day, a value that falls within the range observed for other squalomorph and galeomorph sharks. The thermal regime under which these data were collected is representative of the mean bottom temperatures encountered in the species' core North Sea and Celtic Sea habitats. Such a lengthy gestation imposes significant maternal costs, as females must allocate substantial energy reserves to support developing embryos over nearly two consecutive winter and summer cycles.

Reproductive output for the Starry smooth-hound, when quantified at a prevailing water temperature of 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C], is characterized by an infrequent breeding schedule. Females typically produce one litter every two years [F_R_i = one litter every two years], as recovery from the energetic investment of gestation requires an extended inter-birth interval. This biennial cycle yields a modest annual reproductive output relative to more fecund elasmobranchs like the blue shark, with each pregnancy yielding a complement of 7 to 15 pups [N_R_i = each pregnancy yielding a complement of 7 to 15 pups]. The recovery period between litters is thought to involve replenishment of hepatic lipid stores, which are heavily depleted during embryonic provisioning. This slow pace of reproduction, set against the background temperature, makes the species particularly vulnerable to population declines when subject to elevated adult mortality from fisheries.

Long-term mark-recapture studies have placed the maximum lifespan of the Starry smooth-hound at approximately 18.3 years [am = approximately 18.3 years] when maintained at 10.1 °C [T = 10.1 °C]. This longevity is consistent with a life-history strategy that pairs slow growth and delayed maturation with an extended adult phase, allowing multiple reproductive events across a female's lifetime. Older individuals, particularly those approaching this lifespan limit, exhibit reduced growth increments and a higher incidence of healed predator-inflicted wounds, indicating senescence. The species' lifespan is comparable to that of the closely related Mustelus mustelus, though somewhat shorter than that of larger triakids such as Galeorhinus galeus. Continued monitoring of age structures in wild populations is essential for assessing the impact of chronic fishing pressure on this slow-lived demersal shark.
